assessment_summary:
Step 1: Let G be a finite simple graph that is regular and edge-transitive. We may assume G has at least one edge, as an edgeless graph is trivially vertex-transitive.
Step 2: Since G is edge-transitive, its automorphism group Aut(G) has at most two orbits on the vertices.
Step 3: If Aut(G) has exactly one orbit on the vertices, G is vertex-transitive.
Step 4: If Aut(G) has two orbits, say U and W, then every edge must connect a vertex in U to a vertex in W (if an edge were within U, edge-transitivity would mean all edges are within U, leaving W isolated, contradicting that G is regular with degree > 0). Thus, G is bipartite with parts U and W.
Step 5: Let d be the degree of G. Counting the edges in the bipartite graph gives |U|*d = |W|*d. Since d > 0, this implies |U| = |W|.
Step 6: Since the two bipartite partitions have the same size and all vertices have the same degree, there must exist an automorphism of G that swaps U and W, making G vertex-transitive.

Assessment: Step 6 is flawed. The fact that the two partitions are equal in size and degree does not guarantee the existence of an automorphism that swaps them. Graphs that are regular and edge-transitive but not vertex-transitive do exist; they are known as semi-symmetric graphs (the smallest example being the Folkman graph on 20 vertices).
